media.transcript: Columbus City Schools is getting closer to deciding whether or not all high school students will ride COTA buses to school. This comes after the district looks to cut $50 million from its budget. Columbus City Schools transports more than 32,000 students a year safely to and from school every day. But as we look at our budget for the future, we need to make smart decisions. Thousands of high school students in Columbus could soon see a major change in how they get to and from school as the district considers eliminating yellow buses. Members of a Columbus City Schools Transportation Work Group formed in December 2025 are working to finalize a plan for the future of busing high schoolers in Columbus. So this committee went out to different school facilities. They looked at where are their sidewalks, where are their bus stops, how many transfers could a student need. And what they found is that the vast majority of Columbus City Schools students can ride our current public transit system. At Tuesday night's board meeting, the group presented an update with three potential options for transporting high school students, including those attending charter and private schools. Option one would eliminate both yellow school buses and district-provided COTA passes, leaving families responsible for arranging their own transportation for high schoolers. Option two would eliminate yellow buses and provide high school students with CODA passes. An option three would also eliminate yellow buses and provide students with CODA passes unless a student has more than one transfer. The work group says the proposals could save the district between four and seven million dollars. If that's a system that already works, maybe we don't need to duplicate services with yellow buses. But questions remain about student safety. During Tuesday's meeting, board member Tina Pierce asked the group to provide more details about how students would be kept safe while waiting at bus stops and traveling to and from school. Our high school families are very concerned around safety security at the bus stops. A lot of things are happening at our bus stops. The work group is expected to present its final proposal to the school board in December. Reporting on your site in Columbus, Annabelle Kenney, ABC6 News. Thank you.

media.transcript: As a British person living in France, I am very frustrated by the version of this weekend being fed to people back home and beyond. So let me walk you through what's actually happening. On the 21st of September, kids from a school in Créter, just outside Paris, blockaded their own school gates. Their teachers had left without ever being replaced, their class sizes were too big for the rooms, and the building was falling apart around them. Within weeks, hundreds of schools across the country had closed. What they're asking for is honestly modest. They want teachers recruited at scale, more university places and 10 billion euros to fix crumbling schools. Now that number might sound eye-watering but so is the magnitude of the problem which is why these teenagers are taking to the streets to be heard. Some of them are doing 10 hour school days. No wonder they're exhausted. And everyone else's money is running out too. Fuel has gone through the roof, energy bills are up by about a fifth and the government is trying to push a budget built on cuts months before a presidential election. So on Saturday the Gilets Jeans came back out and the unions came with them. Approximately half a million people marched across France, around 35,000 of them through my city of Montpellier with six formers leading the charge. Now some of it did turn very ugly and I won't pretend otherwise. As you've likely all seen the Limoges town hall was gutted by fire with staff still inside who escaped unharmed. In cities like Paris and Marseille, masked men were smashing up shop fronts. In Montpellier we had some looting and some arson too. The monoprix on the main square had its window put through, shop owners were injured trying to keep these opportunists out, and Foot Locker got looted even though protesters were literally stood in front of it to try and stop that happening. As you might have guessed, these men were not the 16 year olds that have been protesting for weeks. Macron's government has said that organised ultra-left groups were behind a lot of it, and if that's the case, then prosecute them. Just remember, the first people they wronged were the students, whose message they have effectively buried. And I bet you also haven't seen much about how this movement has been policed. For a month, kids have been tear gassed outside their own schools. A 15 year old in Lens lost his hand after police fired a stun grenade. It got so bad the government suspended the use of stun grenades at student protests earlier this month. More than 6,000 people have been arrested, most of them under 18. In Dunkirk, police drove a 4x4 at a crowd of school students and a 14 year old girl ended up in hospital. That same car was paid for by British taxpayers bought under the Sandhurst Treaty to stop people boarding small boats on French beaches. Imagine you're 16 years old for example and you've spent a month being gassed outside of your own school for demanding an adequate education. You're going to be angry. I'm not excusing arson or violence but it's why people's collective anger manifests itself like this and pretending otherwise is how you get the same weekend again. Saturday also happened to be 65 years to the day since Parisian police killed Algerian protesters and threw some of them in the Seine. Here in Montpellier someone tagged a wall with "Ni oubli ni pardon" which translates to "No forgetting, no forgiveness. But from what I've seen the story reaching Britain and beyond is very very different. Old videos from 2017 and 2023 have been passed off as these current protests. A Russian influence campaign has put out fake reports including one claiming the Pope fled France after an attack by Muslims. Like what? Alex Jones said he'd seen a dozen videos of priests being set on fire. A viral clip declaring that France has fallen was actually from a football celebration. Like you get the picture. And to nobody's surprise the bullshitters over at GB News have been misleading their viewers too. For example on Saturday night Alex Armstrong told viewers these protests were down to mass migration and Islamism. The day before he'd agreed at the high court to pay substantial damages to Mothin Ali a Muslim councillor that he'd falsely linked to the Hare Hills riots. Less than 24 hours after apologising for pinning a riot on a Muslim man he was pinning one on Muslims in general. Last Sunday though GB News's own website was blaming the ultra-left instead while also running a story about that British funded 4x4. So it was Islamists on Saturday, ultra-left criminals by Sunday and somehow also children being run over by police. Nobody at that channel ever seems to be able to tell a cohesive story. But the story keeps changing because it was never the point, the footage is. A video of a burning town hall for example is perfect for a news feed because it arrives without any context and whoever shares it gets to dictate what it means and the UK should know because in 2024 a false claim that the Southport attacker was a Muslim asylum seeker led to violent riots within days. It's strange that those acts of delinquency didn't receive the same widespread condemnation from this lot isn't it? Macron addressed the country on Sunday night with most of his speech going to the far left and delinquents and criminals. The hundreds of thousands of regular citizens who marched for legitimate reasons got a passing mention and the promise of a meeting this week. I've seen French people on my timeline very angry that he isn't dealing with why anyone was actually there and I think they're right. Reassuringly though the students aren't backing down. They want to put costed proposals to the Prime Minister himself and the unions have called for a national strike on the 5th of November. These kids have been gassed, arrested by the truckload and told by the incontinent senile President of the United States that they're a front for Islam and yet they're still asking for exactly what they were asking for at the beginning of this which is why they have my full solidarity in doing so. I've written a full piece about this with sources and further context on my website liamromedy.com the link is in my bio if you want to read. Vive la France!

What makes Stanford SO great? 

And what does it actually take to get in?

Intellectual vitality. 

That’s so much of why we built the FlightPlan. How do we cultivate intellectual vitality and build a track record of success to show for it long before senior year comes along? That’s what it takes.

onScreenText: Why is Stanford the best university in the world?
media.transcript: Stanford is arguably the best university in the world. Why? Let's talk about it. First, selectivity. Stanford admission rate is just 3.6%. Getting in is nearly impossible. Second, the resources are insane. Stanford became the top fundraising university in the country and the first to surpass 1 billion raised in a single year. Even if you remove the Stanford hospital system, the university's annual revenue is nearly twice that of Harvard or Yale, despite educating roughly the same number of students. Stanford's annual budget is bigger than that of 116 countries. Third, it's elite across the board: business school, law school, medicine, humanities and sciences, and obviously engineering. Stanford also boasts one of the most influential in-house think tanks of any university. And athletics, it has won the Director's Cup, awarded to the best overall collegiate athletics program in the NCAA, 26 of the 32 times it's been awarded. Fourth, the outcomes speak for themselves. Stanford has produced more 10-figure companies than any other university. And in the most recent Olympics, Stanford athletes won roughly double the medals of the next highest university. So what does it actually take to get in? Intellectual vitality. That is the Stanford admissions thing. Are you deeply curious? And more importantly, what have you done to actually prove that? Because you can't manufacture intellectual vitality senior year. It takes years to explore your interests, go deep, build things, pursue ideas, and create evidence of who you are. And that's exactly why we built the flight plan. So you could be the person who pursues your intellectual vitality long before the college process comes along to help students figure out what they genuinely care about and help them actually do something meaningful with it. Follow along.
